$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{36}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {36}^{{log}_{36}⁡x} & ={36}^{1/2}\end{aligned}

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${36}^{{log}_{36}⁡x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={36}^{1/2} \\ x & =\sqrt{36} \\ x & =6\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}⁡x+2{log}_{8}⁡x & =2 \\ (1+2){log}_{8}⁡x & =2 \\ 3{log}_{8}⁡x & =2 \\ {log}_{8}⁡x & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $8,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}⁡x & =\frac{2}{3} \\ {8}^{{log}_{8}⁡x} & ={8}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${8}^{{log}_{8}⁡x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={8}^{2/3} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{64} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: If $\log_2 x = 5,$ then what is the value of $x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $2,$ so we use a base of $2$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡x & =5 \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}⁡x} & ={2}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $2^{\log_2 x} = x.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{5} \\ x & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(2x+1) & =1 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(2x+1)} & ={7}^{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $7^{\log_7 (2x + 1)} = 2x+1.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & =7 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving Logarithmic Equations by First Rearranging the Equation
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $2\log_5 (x-3)+1 = 5,$ then what is the value of $x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make $\log_5 (x-3)$ the subject of the equation by moving everything else to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{log}_{5}⁡(x-3)+1 & =5 \\ 2{log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =4 \\ {log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $5,$ so we use a base of $5$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡(x-3) & =2 \\ {5}^{{log}_{5}⁡(x-3)} & ={5}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $5^{\log_5 (x - 3)} = x-3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & ={5}^{2} \\ x-3 & =25 \\ x & =28\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving Logarithmic Equations by Combining Logarithmic Terms
canonical_examples.problem: If $7\log_6{x} - 3\log_6{x} = 2,$ then what is the value of  $x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we simplify our equation by collecting the like logarithmic terms, and isolating the logarithm, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{log}_{6}⁡x-3{log}_{6}⁡x & =2 \\ (7-3){log}_{6}⁡x & =2 \\ 4{log}_{6}⁡x & =2 \\ {log}_{6}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $6,$ so we use a base of $6$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{6}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {6}^{{log}_{6}⁡x} & ={6}^{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $6^{\log_6 x} = x.$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={6}^{1/2} \\ x & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we are given the equation $\log_3 x = 4.$ Can we determine $x?$

Recall that the inverse operation of the logarithm is exponentiation. So, to isolate $x,$ we must exponentiate both sides of this equation. 

The base of the logarithm is $3,$ so we use a base of $3$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡x & =4 \\ {3}^{({log}_{3}⁡x)} & ={3}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above may look complicated, but since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we know that $3^{(\log_3{x})}=x.$ Therefore, we get   

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={3}^{4} \\ x & =81.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x = 81$ is the solution.
